Architectural Specification and Operational Framework for Enterprise GitHub Custom Agents and Model Context Protocol IntegrationEnterprise software engineering has evolved beyond static continuous integration scripts toward autonomous agentic workflows capable of performing multi-file edits, executing complex refactoring tasks, and enforcing architectural invariants across distributed repositories. Within large-scale SaaS applications, maintaining architectural discipline across multi-tenant boundaries requires binding generative language models to rigid execution contracts. Custom agent profiles, stored as .agent.md files within repository structures, establish deterministic operational boundaries by combining declarative metadata, allowed tool inventories, and explicit system prompts. When paired with the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and specifically the GitHub MCP Server (github-mcp-server), these custom agents can inspect repositories, modify code bases, validate static analysis boundaries, and execute end-to-end pull request pipelines without human drift or manual oversight.Structural Architecture of Custom Agent ProfilesCustom agent profiles represent declarative persona definitions located within the .github/agents/ directory of a workspace. Each agent profile pairs a YAML frontmatter header with a Markdown system prompt body. The frontmatter dictates runtime discovery, persona handles, argument hints, tool access permissions, model selection, and subagent invocation hierarchies, while the Markdown prompt body provides the behavioral, architectural, and procedural instructions governing agent operations.Unlike global workspace instructions, which apply universally to every conversational interaction, custom agents are activated either by explicit user selection or through automated subagent delegation. This separation prevents context pollution and maintains specialized domain expertise across complex software lifecycles.Frontmatter ParameterData TypeSpecification RequirementBehavioral Impact and Governance FunctionnameStringOptionalSets the explicit invocation name for the agent, defaulting to the base filename if omitted.descriptionStringRequiredServes as the primary delegation string used by agent pickers and parent models to route relevant tasks.argument-hintStringOptionalRenders user interface placeholder text guiding developers on expected input formats.toolsArray of StringsOptionalEnforces a strict allowlist of accessible tools, where omitting the field grants full system tool access.agentsArray of StringsOptionalDefines an explicit allowlist of child custom agents that can be spawned as subagents.modelString / ArrayOptionalPins agent execution to specific foundation models, supporting fallback arrays for resilience.user-invocableBooleanOptionalControls menu visibility, allowing specialized utility agents to be hidden from direct user selection.disable-model-invocationBooleanOptionalBlocks automated subagent delegation, requiring manual human triggering for security-critical tasks.The interaction model relies on system prompt composition. When an agent is invoked, the host environment constructs a system prompt by layering host instructions, custom workspace instructions, and the agent's specific Markdown body. Contextual information regarding operating system parameters and workspace directory trees is appended alongside user prompts and explicitly referenced prompt files. This guarantees that custom agents execute with full contextual awareness while remaining constrained by the explicit rules defined within their profile definitions.Model Context Protocol Integration and Tool ScopingThe Model Context Protocol (MCP) provides a standardized, stateful protocol operating over JSON-RPC 2.0 that connects language model clients to external tools, databases, and service endpoints. Communication occurs either via local standard input/output (stdio) streams for process-isolated local executions or via Streamable HTTP utilizing Server-Sent Events (SSE) for remote microservice integrations.The official GitHub MCP Server (github-mcp-server) wraps GitHub REST and GraphQL APIs into standardized tool endpoints, allowing AI clients to execute repository management, issue tracking, workflow monitoring, and file manipulation through natural language requests. Toolsets are logically categorized to enable fine-grained access control through command-line flags or environment variables, mitigating security risks associated with over-privileged service accounts.MCP Toolset CategoryPrimary Operational ScopeIncluded CapabilitiesSecurity Control MechanismcontextEnvironment Identityget_user, get_contextResolves active user session claims and repository context boundaries.reposRepository Operationscreate_repository, fork_repository, get_commit, create_branchRestricts operations to explicitly authorized organizations and repositories.file_opsFile System Mutationscreate_or_update_file, delete_file, get_file_contentsEnforces path validation and branch protection rules prior to execution.pull_requestsPR Lifecycle Scopingcreate_pull_request, list_pull_requests, merge_pull_requestEnforces automated review checks and structured template validation.issuesIssue Tracker Synccreate_issue, add_issue_comment, list_issuesBinds commit activities to structured issue identifiers and task states.actionsCI/CD Automationlist_workflow_runs, re_run_workflow, get_workflow_runMonitors build status and automated testing pipeline executions.code_securitySecurity Analysislist_code_scanning_alerts, get_alert_detailsBlocks pull request merging if unresolved code scanning alerts exist.secret_protectionVulnerability Guardrailslist_secret_scanning_alertsPrevents token leakages by scanning modified files prior to branch commits.Tool definitions within MCP support behavioral hint annotations that inform client orchestration engines about the safety characteristics of each operation. Annotations such as readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, and openWorldHint allow host applications to enforce user confirmation prompts before executing destructive or non-idempotent operations, providing defense-in-depth against unexpected model behavior.System Architecture Governance and Enforcement RulesIn enterprise Next.js and Redux SaaS applications, autonomous custom agents must adhere to strict layered architecture rules to prevent codebase erosion. Application code is partitioned into business domains within src/features/<module>/, enforcing a strictly downward dependency flow. Higher layers may import from lower layers, but lower layers are strictly prohibited from importing from higher layers.The top layer comprises the App Router (src/app/), containing route segments, layouts, and page entry points. Below the routing layer sits Level 3 Business Features (src/features/*), which encapsulates domain-specific components, Server Actions, repository queries, Zod schemas, TypeScript types, and local feature Redux slices. Beneath business features lies Level 2 Shared Application Primitives (src/components/), containing domain-agnostic composite UI structures such as data tables, filter bars, and modal wrappers. Level 1 UI Primitives (src/components/ui/*) sit near the bottom, housing atomic UI controls installed directly via the shadcn/ui registry. The lowest layer is Level 4 Server Infrastructure (src/server/), housing server-only database adapters, authentication handlers, Redis clients, and external service clients. Cross-cutting shared utilities reside in src/lib/, possessing zero downward dependencies of their own.To prevent context drift, reliance on prompt instructions alone is insufficient. Architectural boundaries must be mechanized using static analysis tools embedded within continuous integration workflows. Layer direction rules are enforced using eslint-plugin-boundaries, flagging disallowed upward or lateral imports as build errors. Deep internal imports into feature modules are forbidden using no-restricted-imports, forcing all cross-feature access to pass exclusively through public barrel exports (src/features/<module>/index.ts).Multi-tenant security requires that every persisted database entity contain a mandatory tenantId field. The tenant identifier must be resolved server-side from session tokens rather than untrusted client payloads and passed explicitly into all query and action functions. Database access is isolated behind repository interfaces (CustomerRepository), enabling the application to operate on an in-memory mock data layer in src/server/db/mock/ during initial development phases while facilitating seamless migration to Neon PostgreSQL and Prisma ORM once infrastructure credentials are deployed. Persistent entities must also support soft-deletion via deletedAt timestamps and optimistic locking via integer version fields to prevent data overwrites during concurrent edits.Every working directory must contain a local specification file named ARCH_SPEC.md. This document records allowed imports, public API exports, state management scopes, and data source statuses. Custom agents are obligated to inspect local ARCH_SPEC.md contracts prior to editing files and must immediately update specification contracts whenever exports, components, schemas, or dependencies are modified.Production Profile Specification for GithubBotThe code block below contains the complete, production-grade custom agent specification file (GithubBot.agent.md) ready for deployment into the .github/agents/ directory. ## 4. Multi-Tenant Security, Input Validation, and Audit Contracts

1. **Input Validation:** Every Server Action and API Route Handler must validate incoming payloads using Zod schemas defined in `src/features/<module>/schemas/` prior to executing business logic.
2. **Tenant Isolation (`tenantId`):**
   - Every domain entity schema must include a mandatory `tenantId` string property.
   - The `tenantId` must be resolved server-side from authenticated session claims—never accepted as an untrusted client parameter.
   - Every query and mutation function must accept and enforce `tenantId` as a mandatory filter parameter.
3. **Audit Trails & Soft Deletion:**
   - Domain entities must maintain `createdAt`, `updatedAt`, `createdBy`, `updatedBy`, and `deletedAt` (nullable soft deletion timestamp) fields.
   - Financial or billing entities subject to concurrent edits must implement optimistic locking via an integer `version` property.
4. **Data Privacy:** Server secrets and environment variables must never be prefixed with `NEXT_PUBLIC_` or imported into client components.

---

## 5. Directory Specification Protocol (`ARCH_SPEC.md`)

Every folder under `src/features/`, `src/components/`, `src/store/`, and `src/server/` must contain a local specification contract titled `ARCH_SPEC.md`.

### Operational Protocol for AI Agents

1. **Inspect Before Editing:** Read the local `ARCH_SPEC.md` prior to creating or modifying code in a directory to verify allowed imports and exported interfaces.
2. **Synchronize Specifications:** Update `ARCH_SPEC.md` under `## Public API Exports` and log the update in `## 6. Maintenance Log` whenever components, actions, schemas, or types are added or modified.
3. **Reconcile Discrepancies:** Reconcile any code-to-spec discrepancies immediately before proceeding with feature development.

---

## 6. Execution Workflow for Task Implementation

Execute software development tasks adhering to the following step-by-step sequence:

1. **Inspect Context:** Read `README.md` and local `ARCH_SPEC.md` files across target directories.
2. **Evaluate UI Primitives:** Check if existing Level 1 (`src/components/ui/`) or Level 2 (`src/components/`) components fulfill visual requirements. If a required Level 1 primitive is missing, execute `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add <component>` prior to writing custom UI code.
3. **Implement Feature Logic:**
   - Define data contracts in `schemas/` using Zod.
   - Declare TypeScript interfaces in `types/`.
   - Implement database repository queries and Server Actions in `queries/` and `actions/`, applying Zod validation and `tenantId` filters.
   - Build domain UI components in `components/`, composing Level 1/2 primitives.
   - Export public interfaces through `index.ts`.
4. **Execute Testing and Static Analysis:**
   - Implement unit and integration tests in `__tests__/` for every Server Action (covering happy paths and validation failure cases).
   - Run `pnpm lint` to verify layer boundary compliance.
   - Run `tsc --noEmit` to verify type safety.
   - Run `pnpm test` to verify test suite execution.
5. **Update Directory Specifications:** Sync affected `ARCH_SPEC.md` files.
6. **Execute Version Control Pipeline:** Push updates on a dedicated feature branch (`feature/<module>-<description>`) and submit a pull request utilizing Conventional Commit message syntax.

---

## 7. Definition of Done Checklist

A task is marked complete only when all checklist criteria are satisfied:

- [ ] Local `ARCH_SPEC.md` files inspected, updated, and logged.
- [ ] Server Actions and Route Handlers validate inputs via Zod schemas.
- [ ] Database queries enforce mandatory `tenantId` filtering.
- [ ] UI components strictly adhere to downward layer boundaries.
- [ ] Public interfaces cleanly exported via feature barrel (`index.ts`).
- [ ] Zero TypeScript errors or `any` type overrides exist (`tsc --noEmit` passes).
- [ ] Static analysis passes with zero architecture violations (`pnpm lint` passes).
- [ ] Vitest unit tests created for all Server Actions and schemas (`pnpm test` passes).
- [ ] Change reported using the Standardized Change Reporting Format.

---

## 8. Standardized Change Reporting Format

Upon completing a task, deliver your operational report using this exact template:

ADDED: (List newly created files, components, actions, or schemas)
CHANGED: (List modified files or refactored functions)
REMOVED: (List deprecated or deleted files)
DATABASE: (Status of mock repositories / schema.prisma parity)
ARCH_SPEC: (List ARCH_SPEC.md files updated during execution)
TESTS: (List test suites created or verified)
GIT: (Branch name, Conventional Commit message, and PR submission link)Strategic Synthesis and Operational FrameworkDeploying autonomous agents within enterprise SaaS development environments bridges high-level architectural mandates with granular code modifications. Custom agent profiles defined via Markdown files (.agent.md) form a deterministic operational framework when integrated with the Model Context Protocol. By constraining tool capabilities through allowlists and enforcing clear frontmatter configuration parameters, organizations protect core repositories against unauthorized modifications while providing AI models with the exact tools necessary for complex software engineering.The dual-layer governance model—combining cognitive prompts with mechanized static analysis—guarantees that architectural integrity is preserved over time. Prompt instructions establish structural priorities, data contracts, and design principles, while static analysis rules configured through eslint-plugin-boundaries and no-restricted-imports physically prevent non-compliant code from passing automated CI/CD builds. Simultaneously, the per-directory ARCH_SPEC.md specification protocol solves context drift by maintaining localized memory across iterative development cycles.Abstracting data operations behind repository interfaces ensures that initial feature engineering proceeds rapidly using in-memory mock datasets without incurring early cloud database infrastructure costs or schema lock-in. When production environments are initialized, transitioning from mock stores to live Neon PostgreSQL instance databases using Prisma ORM requires updating localized server adapters, leaving business logic, Zod validation schemas, UI primitives, and test suites completely intact. This comprehensive architectural approach establishes a scalable foundation for AI-assisted enterprise software development.
